prize_parts.citation: for a poetic and essayistic oeuvre that renews lyric, verse narrative and the book itself through a learned and emotionally charged encounter with antiquity, grief and desire

statement.case_for: I keep Anne Carson first on the criteria of voice, formal achievement and imaginative depth. Autobiography of Red turns Stesichorus into a modern verse novel. Nox builds an elegy for a brother out of a translation of Catullus 101, archival fragments and the folded book-object. In both, the formal invention is what carries the emotion, so it is not ornament added to a theme. The classical learning, the translations and the essays feed the poetry. That makes the whole body of work a single practice, and I do not see it as a poet with a scholarly sideline. The voice is recognisable within a few lines, the work has developed across decades, and it extends the possibilities of lyric and prose rather than repeating one gesture. Cărtărescu is the strongest alternative for me. His visionary Romanian prose has a larger imaginative scale, and I would not call it a lesser achievement. But the claim for Carson rests on a more varied formal range, and her work keeps changing shape.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that much of Carson's effect depends on typography, page design, material form and a dialogue with ancient Greek texts. Those may survive only partly in translation and in ordinary editions. A committee reading in Swedish, English and other languages may be judging a partial image of the work. There is also a real question, raised by several colleagues, whether a hybrid, scholarly and sometimes fragmentary body of work answers to the 'ideal direction' of Nobel's will. Formal radicalism and erudition could be mistaken for sustained depth. I have not re-read the texts and have not independently verified any source. My view rests on public knowledge of the major books.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second. He asks how much of Carson's oeuvre is original creation as against translation and adaptation, and whether the formal play is sometimes mannered.
responses.response: I take the question about translation and adaptation seriously, and I think it affects how the citation must be drafted. In Carson, however, the translations and versions of Greek texts are not a separate activity beside the original books. In Nox the act of translating Catullus 101 is the elegiac form itself, and in Autobiography of Red the reworking of Stesichorus becomes an original narrative. So I would credit the original books as the core and treat the translations as part of the same practice. I accept the point about mannerism as a risk in the more occasional later work. I cannot settle it without a closer reading of that work, but the central books show the formal play doing real expressive work. I also agree with his case for Cărtărescu's scale and voice, and I keep him as my first alternative.

responses.point: Swärd also ranks Carson first. She notes that the work is dense, allusive and hard to judge in translation. She asks whether a hybrid form counts as idealistic literature in the sense of Nobel's will or is more a scholarly-poetic achievement.
responses.response: I share her uncertainty about translation and I do not think the committee can wave it away. On the question of 'ideal direction', I would read it through what the work does rather than through its genre. Nox is a sustained act of mourning that remains emotionally exposed beneath its scholarly apparatus, and Autobiography of Red is a coming-of-age story of desire and difference. These are human concerns of broad significance, and they are not specialist ones. Where I would qualify her view is that learnedness is not itself the ideal element. The case holds only if the emotional and imaginative depth is what readers carry away, and that is what I judge to be true of the central books.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second. She stresses his sustained visionary project across novels, poetry and essays, and notes that Carson's work is partly material and visual and is hard to bound as a single-genre claim.
responses.response: I agree that Cărtărescu's achievement is a single coherent world and that his late-career books remain ambitious. I also agree that Carson's scope is harder to bound, and a citation would have to name poetry, essay and verse narrative together. I think that is manageable, because the hybrid method is itself the unifying element. Where I differ is on how to weigh scale. Cărtărescu's strength is the size and density of one vision. Carson's is the repeated invention of new forms, and I weigh the second more heavily because it shows range as well as intensity. Neither of us can fully judge the Romanian sentence in translation, so I would not use that gap against him. It remains an open limit on both of our judgements.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first. She notes that the corpus is smaller and more fragmentary than that of many novelists and that the formal radicalism sometimes sits at the edge of what is read as a genre. She asks how much weight concentrated formal work should carry against bulk.
responses.response: I agree that the corpus is more fragmentary than a novelist's, and I do not want to hide that. I would answer that the prize looks for the quality and significance of the work and does not measure volume. The relevant question is whether the concentrated books are sustained across decades, and public knowledge of the central works suggests they are. Her point that some formal experiments may be judged as erudite play is the strongest version of my own reservation. I cannot dismiss it from public knowledge alone. It is the reason I would want the committee to test the later books before settling on the citation.

uncertainties: How much of Carson's effect, which relies on layout, typography and book-object form, survives in translation and in standard editions.
Whether the later and more occasional work keeps the level of the central books such as Autobiography of Red and Nox. This has not been independently checked.
Whether the committee can phrase one citation that covers poetry, essay, verse narrative, translation and drama without either overstating or narrowing the claim.
Whether Cărtărescu's visionary Romanian prose carries its full force in translation, and how the poetry and early work compare with the major novels. My coverage of that corpus is partial.
Whether Michon's compact oeuvre meets the whole-oeuvre standard. Its main strength lies in French sentence texture that I cannot judge through translation.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile.
